description: Before dreaming of navigating Mars, we learned to read the golden steppes of Central Anatolia—our 'Yellow Sea.' This harsh, beautiful landscape inspires our vision. We aim to conceptualize the safest, most efficient survival routes across Martian terrain. By exploring how astronauts can overcome extreme environments, we want to turn an alien world's challenges into a navigable path for humanity.
summary:
Unlike Earth, there's no GPS system on Mars and the Red Planet presents extreme environmental hazards such as deep canyons, steep craters, dried riverbeds, and high cosmic radiation. That is where KIZA-NAV steps in. KIZA-NAV is an interactive 3D navigation and route-planning web application designed to guide astronauts and rovers safely across the Martian surface.

By integrating high-resolution topographic and orbital datasets from NASA and ESA -specifically MOLA, HRSC, and HiRISE - our KIZA-NAV web application maps the Martian terrain in high detail.

Scientific data about Mars exists in massive, fragmented datasets that are difficult for astronauts to use directly during a mission. KIZA-NAV is important because it unites this complex orbital information into a clear, practical navigation format. By making critical terrain, radiation, and geological data instantly readable on one map, our platform saves valuable mission time and helps explorers make safe, informed decisions on the Martian surface.
details:
What Does KIZA-NAV Do?

Kıza-nav is an interactive 3D web application that transforms NASA and ESA datasets into a GPS-style navigation map for Mars. We designed this web application for astronauts and rovers. Kıza-nav combines terrain elevation and geological landmarks into toggleable layers to guide safe and scientifically valuable Marswalks.

How Does It Work?

  • To show locations on Mars, KIZA-NAV uses the planet’s Areographic and Areocentric coordinate systems (Latitude/Longitude). Since WebGIS tools like CesiumJS normally work on Earth’s WGS84 ellipsoid, we adjusted our Mars surface maps (MOLA and HiRISE) to fit the 3D globe using the EPSG:4326 projection standard. This setup keeps the app fast in web browsers and loads Mars map data into 3D without losing any detail.
    • Local High-Resolution Zone (Jezero Crater): For Jezero Crater, NASA HiRISE imagery is converted into a grayscale matrix. Our A* pathfinding algorithm reads the pixel intensity values in the Red channel (0–255) directly as elevation (Z-axis) traversal costs to compute safe, optimal routes.
    • Global Low-Resolution Zone (Planet-Wide): When navigating outside Jezero Crater's boundaries, the system dynamically fetches NASA’s MOLA colorized elevation map via USGS Web Map Service (WMS). Our custom algorithm reverse-engineers the the color-coded map into real-time height numbers, so the app can easily add global terrain data to its route math.
  • To calculate safe routes for astronauts and rovers, KIZA-NAV uses a custom A* (A-star) pathfinding algorithm over these height grids. Rather than simply computing the shortest straight-line distance, the algorithm evaluates the Z-axis elevation difference between adjacent grid pixels as a traversal cost. Steep crater walls, deep canyons, and sudden drops get much higher movement costs. This steers the route away from dangerous obstacles and onto flatter, safer ground.
  • All spatial data is organized into a synchronized, layered 3D interface powered by CesiumJS. Explorers and mission planners can toggle between orbital imagery and topographic elevation layers, inspect terrain relief from any 3D camera angle, and select custom start and destination waypoints. Once waypoints are placed, KIZA-NAV renders the optimized route directly onto the 3D Martian surface, providing immediate visual clarity for surface traverses.
  • Beyond safe transit, KIZA-NAV supports NASA’s goal of conducting science during Marswalks by highlighting geologically significant landmarks - such as ancient dried riverbeds, delta formations, and crater rims - directly within the navigation view. This allows explorers to align their safest transit paths with high-priority scientific targets on a single unified map.

    What Benefits Does KIZA-NAV Have?

  • High-Performance Browser Accessibility: By converting pixel color values into an Image-Based Elevation Matrix instead of loading heavy DEM files, KIZA-NAV runs smoothly in standard web browsers without lag or high hardware requirements.
  • Unified Data Experience: It eliminates the need for astronauts and mission planners to switch between complex, fragmented scientific tools by merging NASA (HiRISE, MOLA) and ESA datasets into a single, intuitive 3D map.
  • Safer Surface Traverses: Our slope-weighted A* pathfinding algorithm evaluates Z-axis elevation changes to help explorers avoid dangerous crater walls, deep canyons, and steep terrain.
  • Seamless Local-to-Global Scale: Users benefit from both ultra-detailed local navigation inside Jezero Crater and uninterrupted planet-wide route planning in one continuous interface.
  • Maximized Scientific Value: By highlighting geologically significant landmarks—such as ancient dried riverbeds and crater rims—along safe routes, KIZA-NAV turns every Marswalk into a productive scientific expedition.

    What Is The Intended Impact Of The Project?

  • Empowering Intuitive Surface Navigation: By eliminating the need for heavy, specialized GIS software during surface operations, KIZA-NAV gives astronauts and mission planners immediate visual clarity through a simple, GPS-style web interface.
  • Supporting Future Mars Habitats: Reliable surface routing lays the groundwork for selecting safe base locations and establishing logistics corridors for long-term human presence on the Red Planet.
  • Open Science & Education: Because KIZA-NAV runs smoothly in any standard web browser without heavy hardware, it makes official NASA and ESA exploration data accessible to students, educators, and citizen scientists worldwide.

 What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did We Use To Develop Your Project?

Coding Languages & Web Standards

  • JavaScript (ES6 Modules): Core application logic, state management, asynchronous API handling, and algorithmic pathfinding.
  • HTML5 & CSS3: Modular UI architecture featuring a custom Fluent Design System (glassmorphism, CSS variables, responsive flyouts, and modals) and HTML5 Canvas API for dynamic pixel-level elevation extraction and custom waypoint pin rendering.

Libraries, Engines & Algorithms

  • CesiumJS (v1.111): WebGL-based 3D planetary globe rendering, ellipsoidal horizon occlusion, camera flight physics, and spatial entity management.
  • Custom Topographic Pathfinding Engine: Implemented an 8-way A* (A-Star) search algorithm weighted by non-linear slope penalties, combined with line-of-sight string-pulling (zig-zag pruning) and Chaikin’s corner-cutting algorithm for smooth trajectory generation.

Data Sources, APIs & GIS Pipeline

  • USGS Planetary Maps WMS: Real-time global Mars MOLA (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter) color topography tiles.
  • NASA HiRISE Datasets: High-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data and XYZ map tiles for Jezero Crater.
  • NASA Mars 2020 Raw Images API: Live telemetry and raw image retrieval for the Perseverance Rover and Ingenuity Helicopter.
  • GIS & Image Processing Tools: Used QGIS and GDAL to process raw planetary elevation rasters, generate XYZ tile pyramids (hirise_tiles), and bake grayscale heightmaps (jezero_hirise.png) for client-side pathfinding.

Software & Hardware

  • Software: Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub (version control and deployment), modern Chromium/WebGL-enabled browsers for testing and profiling, and AI/digital illustration tools for the Captain Ferit mission guide mascot.
  • Hardware: Standard consumer development PC/laptop (client-side architecture requires zero specialized server hardware, running entirely in the user's browser via WebGL).

How Is Our Project Creative?

The creativity of KIZA-NAV lies in transforming intimidating, scientist-only planetary data into a familiar, everyday GPS experience for future Mars explorers. Instead of relying on heavy, slow-loading 3D terrain files that require powerful computers, we took an out-of-the-box approach by teaching our system to read elevation directly from visual map colors, making complex Martian landscapes run smoothly on any standard browser. Furthermore, rather than treating navigation merely as finding the shortest line between two points, we reimagined route planning as a balance between human safety and scientific curiosity—guiding astronauts around steep hazards while highlighting fascinating geological landmarks to explore along the way.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

While designing KIZA-NAV, our team focused on four main factors: crew safety, browser performance, ease of use, and scientific value. First, Mars has extreme terrain hazards like steep crater walls and deep canyons, so we prioritized slope safety by making our pathfinding algorithm penalize sharp elevation changes. Second, raw planetary elevation files (DEMs) are massive and easily freeze standard computers, so we considered hardware limits and built our lightweight Image-Based Elevation Matrix to keep the app fast in any browser. Third, astronauts and planners need quick answers during a mission, so we designed a clean, GPS-style 3D interface instead of a complicated scientific tool. Finally, because Marswalks are meant for discovery, we factored in how to guide explorers near interesting geological sites like dried riverbeds without compromising their safety.
